blocks.title: Condensation polymerisation
blocks.text: In condensation polymerisation, monomers join together and, each time a new bond forms, a small molecule is eliminated, usually water but sometimes HCl, CH3OH or NH3. The monomers must have at least two reactive functional groups (such as -OH, -COOH or -NH2), on different ends of the monomer(s), and the polymer grows step by step.

blocks.alt: Top: two kinds of monomer, H-X-H and HO-Y-OH. Middle: the monomers lined up alternately, with H+HO and OH+H between them boxed as the parts that leave. Bottom: H-X-Y-X-Y-OH + 3H2O.
blocks.caption: The idea of condensation polymerisation (original diagram after Figure 26.3).
blocks.long_description: Each monomer has a reactive group at both ends. Wherever two monomers meet, an H from one and an OH from the other leave as water and a new bond joins the monomers, so four monomers give a chain and three molecules of water.

blocks.text: Polyesters have ester links (-CO-O-) in their backbone. A diol (two -OH groups) and a dicarboxylic acid (two -COOH groups) combine to give a polyester: an -OH of the diol reacts with a -COOH of the acid and water is removed. Terylene (PET) is made from ethane-1,2-diol and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid.

blocks.alt: Ethane-1,2-diol, HOCH2CH2OH, + benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid, HOOC-C6H4-COOH; H from the diol and -OH from the acid leave as water, giving the bracketed repeat unit -O-CH2CH2-O-CO-C6H4-CO- of PET, joined by ester links.
blocks.caption: Making the polyester PET (original diagram after the book's scheme).
blocks.long_description: Each ester link forms between one end of a diol and one end of a diacid, with the loss of one water molecule. Because both monomers have two reactive ends, the chain can keep growing in both directions.

blocks.text: Polyesters have high tensile strength, which makes them suitable for fibres; polyester is used as an alternative to cotton because of its low cost and resistance to creasing. It is also used as a plastic, for example PET (PETE) bottles for drinks and food packaging, and as cross-links in hard plastics such as glass-fibre-reinforced cross-linked polyester.

items: From a diamine and a dicarboxylic acid: the -NH2 of the diamine reacts with the -COOH of the acid and water is removed: n H2N-R-NH2 + n HOOC-R'-COOH -> [-HN-R-NH-CO-R'-CO-]n + n H2O. Nylon-6,6 uses hexane-1,6-diamine (hexamethylenediamine) and hexanedioic (adipic) acid.
From a diamine and a dioyl chloride (two -COCl groups), which are more reactive than dicarboxylic acids; hydrogen chloride is removed: n H2N-R-NH2 + n ClOC-R'-COCl -> [-HN-R-NH-CO-R'-CO-]n + n HCl.

From an amino acid, a single monomer with both -NH2 and -COOH: the -NH2 of one molecule reacts with the -COOH of another, removing water and forming a peptide bond, a kind of amide link: n H2N-CH2-COOH -> [-HN-CH2-CO-]n + n H2O. Proteins are natural polyamides made from amino acids (Chapter 27).

blocks.text: Amide links also form between an acyl chloride and ammonia or an amine (such as methanamine, CH3NH2, or N-methylmethanamine, (CH3)2NH), with loss of hydrogen chloride: R-COCl + R'-NH2 -> R-CO-NH-R' + HCl. This happens easily at room temperature because acyl chlorides are very reactive.

blocks.alt: Four panels of general equations: diamine + dicarboxylic acid giving a polyamide and water; diamine + dioyl chloride giving a polyamide and HCl; an amino acid giving a polyamide and water; an acyl chloride + an amine giving an amide R-CO-NH-R' and HCl.
blocks.caption: Ways of forming polyamides and amide links (original summary of the book's equations).
blocks.long_description: In every case an -NH2 group and a carbonyl group (from -COOH or -COCl) join to form an amide link, -CO-NH-, and a small molecule, water or HCl, is lost. The book writes the monomers with a single CH2 group between the reactive groups; real monomers, such as those of nylon-6,6, have longer chains.

blocks.prompt: What small molecule is lost when a diamine reacts with a dioyl chloride, and why is the dioyl chloride used?
blocks.explanation: Hydrogen chloride; dioyl chlorides are much more reactive than dicarboxylic acids, so the reaction goes easily at room temperature.

items: Condensation: a small molecule (H2O, HCl) is lost at each link; monomers need two reactive groups.
Polyamides (-CONH-): diamine + diacid or dioyl chloride, or amino acids.
